blogs.title: Don't Forget the Dog: Capnocytophaga canimorsus and the Septic Patient with a Bite History
blogs.description: This post explores Capnocytophaga canimorsus as a rare but potentially devastating pathogen following dog bites. We discuss its fastidious, slow-growing nature that delays blood culture identification, the broad spectrum of presentations from isolated meningitis to fulminant sepsis with DIC, and why early empiric coverage with broad-spectrum antibiotics (such as piperacillin-tazobactam) is critical when a dog bite history is present. We also examine the rising role of molecular diagnostics like nanopore sequencing in accelerating diagnosis, and review mortality rates approaching 30% despite broad antibiotic susceptibility.

blogs.title: When Sepsis Improves But Haemolysis Worsens: Recognizing Superimposed Thrombotic Microangiopathy
blogs.description: This post focuses on the clinical pattern recognition challenge when a patient with resolving sepsis and DIC suddenly develops new isolated haemolysis, worsening thrombocytopenia, and persistent AKI. We discuss how the initial sepsis picture can obscure a superimposed TMA, the importance of sending a peripheral smear for schistocytes when haemolysis doesn't fit the clinical trajectory, and the pitfalls of a falsely positive DAT (Coombs test) due to penicillin exposure or transfusions leading clinicians down an autoimmune haemolytic anaemia pathway. The post emphasizes temporal pattern recognition as a key diagnostic tool.

blogs.title: MAHA + Thrombocytopenia + AKI: Navigating the TMA Diagnostic Maze
blogs.description: This post walks through the structured differential diagnosis of thrombotic microangiopathy in adults, using this case as a framework. We review how to systematically exclude TTP (ADAMTS13 activity <10%, PLASMIC score), STEC-HUS (stool PCR for Shiga toxin, prodromal enteric illness), and secondary TMA from drugs, autoimmune disease, and malignant hypertension. We discuss why a kidney biopsy can be invaluable in confirming TMA and guiding subtype classification, and how renal biopsy findings of ischaemic glomeruli with fibrin thrombi and crescent formation fit into the broader TMA spectrum.

blogs.title: Normal C3 and C4 Do Not Exclude Complement-Mediated HUS: A Critical Diagnostic Pitfall
blogs.description: This post addresses the dangerous misconception that normal complement levels rule out CM-HUS. We discuss how C3 and C4 may remain within reference ranges throughout the disease course, how CM-HUS is ultimately a clinicopathological diagnosis of exclusion, and why relying on standard complement panels alone is insufficient. We also examine the challenges of interpreting extended complement testing (such as alternative pathway AH50) when performed after plasma exchange and eculizumab have already been initiated, and how treatment effects can mimic or mask intrinsic complement dysregulation.

blogs.title: Complement Blockade in the Face of Active Bacteraemia: Walking the Therapeutic Tightrope
blogs.description: This post examines the clinical dilemma of initiating eculizumab—a terminal complement inhibitor—in a patient with recent or ongoing bacteraemia. We discuss how terminal complement is critical for defence against encapsulated organisms like Neisseria and Capnocytophaga, the importance of confirming culture negativity before initiation, the essential role of meningococcal vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis, and the use of plasma exchange as a bridging strategy. We also review evidence on time-to-eculizumab as a determinant of renal recovery, weighing the urgency of complement blockade against infectious risk.

blogs.title: Infection-Triggered CM-HUS Without a Genetic Predisposition: Rethinking the 'Second Hit' Model
blogs.description: This post explores the pathophysiology of complement-mediated HUS triggered by infection in the absence of identified complement gene variants. We discuss the classical 'second hit' model—where a genetic predisposition requires an external trigger like infection to manifest disease—and how this case challenges that framework by demonstrating CM-HUS with no pathogenic complement variants identified. We review the proposed mechanisms by which C. canimorsus may directly activate complement pathways, the paradox of complement activation clearing the pathogen while simultaneously driving endothelial damage, and the implications for prognosis, relapse risk, and decisions about long-term eculizumab maintenance.
